title: Who did it? Active and passive sentences
examples: How do I turn an active sentence into passive?
When should I use the passive?

stages.label: by + the doer
stages.note: The cake was eaten by the dog.

explain.say: Imagine you come home and the birthday cake is gone. You can say: The dog ate the cake. Or: The cake was eaten! Look at the first box on the board. The dog ate the cake is active: the doer, the dog, comes first.

draw.text: Who did it? Active and passive sentences

stages.label: by + the doer
stages.note: The cake was eaten by the dog.

explain.say: Now let's flip it, one move at a time. See the second box? Move the thing that got eaten, the cake, to the front. The cake... Now the sentence is about the cake, not the dog.

stages.label: by + the doer
stages.note: The cake was eaten by the dog.

explain.say: The third box adds a helper verb, was or were. The cake was... Then look at the fourth box: the verb changes to its past participle, eaten. The cake was eaten. Can you hear the change?

stages.label: by + the doer
stages.note: The cake was eaten by the dog.

explain.say: Last box: add by and the doer: The cake was eaten by the dog. That whole flipped sentence is passive. The doer is at the end, or can even disappear. Who ate it? We don't have to say!

stages.label: by + the doer
stages.note: The cake was eaten by the dog.

explain.say: Well done! Writers use the passive when the doer is unknown or less important, like The Taj Mahal was built in the 1600s. Look at the board one more time. Challenge: make this passive: Kemi painted the fence.

stages.label: by + the doer
stages.note: The cake was eaten by the dog.

faq.a: In the active voice the doer comes first and does the action: The dog ate the cake. It is clear and direct.
In the passive voice the thing the action happens to comes first, with was or were and a past participle: The cake was eaten by the dog.

faq.q: How do I turn an active sentence into passive?
faq.a: Move the object to the front, add was or were, change the verb to its past participle, then add by and the doer if you want.

faq.q: When should I use the passive?
faq.a: Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or less important, as in My bike was stolen, or in science reports: The water was heated.
It is the verb form used after has or was: eaten, built, painted, written. For regular verbs it ends in ed.

facts: Science reports often use the passive, as in The solution was heated, to focus on what happened rather than who did it.
The Taj Mahal was built in the 1600s, a passive sentence where the builders are not named.

options.show: The window was broken by a ball.
options.say: The window was broken by a ball.

quiz.why: Was broken plus by a ball makes it passive.

wrong.0: Here the doer, a ball, comes first: active.
wrong.2: This has no was plus past participle.

quiz.say: Make it passive: Kemi painted the fence.
quiz.show: Make it passive: Kemi painted the fence.

options.show: Kemi was painted by the fence.
options.say: Kemi was painted by the fence.

options.show: The fence was painted by Kemi.
options.say: The fence was painted by Kemi.

quiz.why: Object first, add was, past participle painted, then by Kemi.

wrong.1: This is still active, and it changes the meaning.
